modules.name: Counting
modules.header:
The two counting distributions, each exact at every parameter.
Both have a direct method that is obviously right and obviously unusable past a modest parameter, and both
have a reduction that hands the large case to the gamma family. The reductions are Devroye's: they are exact
rather than approximate, and they recurse logarithmically rather than looping once per unit of the parameter.

modules.name: Distribution
modules.header:
The distributions every simulation needs first.
Each is generated by the method that is correct rather than the one that is shortest, and where those differ
the reason is written down. The recurring hazard is the same one: a transform that is exact in real arithmetic
can be catastrophically wrong in floating point at the edge of its input range, because the generator will
eventually produce the edge.

modules.name: Extract
modules.header:
Everything that is not a 64-bit word, derived from the stream of 64-bit words.
These live here rather than on each generator so that two different generators seeded alike agree on more
than their raw output: the same word stream yields the same bytes, the same narrow integers and the same
floats, whichever algorithm produced it. A generator that supplied its own byte extraction would be free to
disagree, and the disagreement would only show up as an unreproducible result somewhere far away.

modules.name: Gamma
modules.header:
The gamma family, and the two counting distributions built on it.
These are the distributions where the shortest correct method is not obvious, and where the usual shortcuts
are wrong in ways that only show up in the tail. Summing `n` Bernoulli draws for a binomial is exact but takes
`n` draws, which is unusable for the large `n` that makes a binomial interesting. Multiplying uniforms for a
Poisson is exact but takes about `lambda` draws and underflows to a hang for a large mean. And a normal
approximation to either is not the distribution at all — it is a different one that happens to look similar
near the middle.
So each is exact at every parameter, and each reduces to the gamma distribution when its parameter grows: the
binomial through a beta split that halves the problem, and the Poisson through a gamma step that consumes a
large chunk of the mean at once. Both are Devroye's constructions, and both recurse only logarithmically.

modules.name: Generator
modules.header:
What a random generator is, and how one is seeded.
A generator is borrowed mutably for every draw, either as its concrete type through a generic bound or as a
borrowed interface view. Both forms refer to the caller's original generator, so advancing it here advances
the state the caller observes. Generic bounds retain static dispatch for the distribution helpers without
forcing callers to expose a raw pointer.
Everything is built on one primitive, `NextUint64`, because every other shape — bytes, narrower words,
bounded integers, floats — is a deterministic function of a stream of 64-bit words. Deriving them here rather
than letting each generator supply its own is what makes two generators seeded alike produce the same
sequence of *values*, not merely the same sequence of words.

modules.name: Pcg64
modules.header:
PCG64-DXSM, a generator with a 128-bit linear congruential state and a strong output function.
The state advances by an ordinary multiply-and-add in 128 bits, which is trivially predictable on its own;
everything that makes the output good happens in the output function, which folds the high half through two
multiplications and finishes by multiplying by the low half. DXSM is the "double xorshift multiply" variant
that replaced the original PCG64 output after the latter was shown to have a weakness at extreme sample
sizes, and it is what NumPy adopted as its default.
The period is 2^128 per stream, and the increment selects the stream: two generators with different odd
increments walk different orbits of the same size, which is what makes independent parallel streams possible
without any coordination between them.
**Not suitable for anything that must resist an adversary.** The output function is not invertible in one
step, but nothing here is designed against an attacker who is trying.

modules.name: Reservoir
modules.header:
Sampling from a stream whose length is not known until it ends.
The reservoir is the point: a caller that could hold the whole stream would shuffle it and take a prefix
instead. This keeps only the sample, so a stream of any length — a file being read, a query being scanned --
costs the memory of the answer rather than the memory of the input.

modules.name: Sample
modules.header:
Choosing from a collection: uniformly, by weight, and from a stream whose length is not known in advance.
Each of these has a famous wrong version. A shuffle written as "for each position, swap with a random position
anywhere" is not uniform — it produces n^n equally likely swap sequences over n! permutations, and since n!
does not divide n^n some permutations come out more often. Weighted choice written as a linear scan over
running totals is correct but reads the weights twice and drifts when they are large. Reservoir sampling done
by collecting everything first is not reservoir sampling at all, and defeats the only reason to use it.

modules.name: Seeding
modules.header:
Seeding from the operating system's entropy, and the global generator that deliberately does not exist.
**There is no default generator here, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** A global mutable
generator is convenient and costs three things worth more than the convenience. It makes results
irreproducible, because any library that draws from it shifts every subsequent draw a caller thought was
theirs. It makes correctness depend on threading, because two threads sharing one state either race or
serialize, and the fix for either is worse than passing a generator. And it makes seeding a global decision,
so a program that wants one deterministic component and one entropy-seeded one cannot have both.
A caller who wants one generator for a whole program can make one and pass it. That is one parameter, and it
buys reproducibility, thread independence and per-component seeding all at once.

modules.name: Uniform
modules.header:
Uniform values in a range, without the bias the obvious methods introduce.
`NextUint64() % bound` is the method everyone reaches for and it is not uniform unless `bound` divides 2^64.
With a bound of three, the words 0, 1, 2 map to 0, 1, 2 and so on, but the final partial block leaves one or
two extra chances at the low residues — a bias of about `bound / 2^64`, invisible for small bounds and
glaring for bounds near the width. `(NextFloat64() * bound) as uint64` is worse: it rounds, so it is biased
even for bounds that divide evenly, and it can return `bound` itself at the top.
The method here is Lemire's. Multiply the word by the bound in double width; the high half is already the
answer, and the low half says which part of the block it came from. Only when the low half falls inside the
first `2^64 mod bound` values is the answer possibly from the short block, and only then is a word rejected
and another drawn. The rejection test is exact and the expected number of extra draws is far below one.

modules.name: Xoshiro
modules.header:
Xoshiro256**, a small fast generator with a 256-bit state.
The state is four words and the step is shifts and exclusive-ors, which is why it is fast; the output goes
through two multiplications, which is what makes it pass the statistical tests the raw state would fail. Its
period is 2^256 - 1, and the all-zero state is the one state outside the cycle — it maps to itself forever --
so seeding refuses to leave it there.
Suitable for simulation, shuffling and sampling. **Not suitable for anything that must resist an adversary:**
its output reveals its state, and a few consecutive words are enough to predict every word after them.

items.name: Binomial
items.signature: pub func Binomial<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, trials: uint64, probability: float64) -> uint64

doc.summary: The number of successes in `trials` independent trials each succeeding with probability `probability`.
doc.markdown:
The number of successes in `trials` independent trials each succeeding with probability `probability`.
A probability at or below zero gives zero successes and one at or above one gives every trial, matching
`Bernoulli`'s treatment of the same edges. Zero trials give zero.
Small counts are summed directly, which is the definition. Large ones are split by a beta draw: the median
trial's success probability has a beta distribution, and comparing it to `probability` says which side the
answer falls on and leaves a strictly smaller problem. That halves the count each step, so a binomial over a
billion trials costs about thirty draws rather than a billion.
doc.returns: how many of `trials` succeeded

items.name: Poisson
items.signature: pub func Poisson<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, mean: float64) -> uint64

doc.summary: The number of events in one interval when they arrive independently at the given mean rate.
doc.markdown:
The number of events in one interval when they arrive independently at the given mean rate.
A mean at or below zero gives zero. A small mean uses Knuth's method — multiply uniforms until the product
falls below `exp(-mean)` — which costs about `mean` draws and is exact. A large mean would cost too many
draws that way, and the product would underflow to zero before the loop ended, so the mean is consumed in
chunks: a gamma draw of integer shape is the waiting time for that many events, and either it overshoots the
interval, in which case the count is a binomial of what is left, or it fits and the remainder carries on.
doc.returns: a draw from the Poisson distribution with that mean

items.name: Bernoulli
items.signature: pub func Bernoulli<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, probability: float64) -> bool

doc.summary: A coin that comes up `true` with probability `probability`.
doc.markdown:
A coin that comes up `true` with probability `probability`.
A probability at or below zero never comes up true and one at or above one always does, so a caller
computing a probability that drifts slightly out of range gets the sensible answer rather than an
occasional inversion. The comparison is against a draw in `[0, 1)`, so a probability of exactly zero is
impossible rather than merely rare — which is what makes the two ends behave.
doc.returns: true with the given probability

items.name: Exponential
items.signature: pub func Exponential<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> float64

doc.summary: A value from the exponential distribution with rate one.
doc.markdown:
A value from the exponential distribution with rate one.
The inverse-transform method: the negated logarithm of a uniform draw. Written on `1 - u` rather than on `u`
because `NextFloat64` can return exactly zero, whose logarithm is an infinity — so the draw that would
produce an infinite sample is instead the one that produces zero, which the distribution does allow.
Multiply the result by a mean, or divide by a rate, to scale it.
doc.returns: a draw from the exponential distribution with rate one

items.name: ExponentialWithRate
items.signature: pub func ExponentialWithRate<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, rate: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A value from the exponential distribution with the given rate.
doc.markdown:
A value from the exponential distribution with the given rate.
A rate at or below zero has no distribution and gives zero.

params.name: rate
params.markdown: the distribution's rate, which is the reciprocal of its mean

doc.returns: a draw from the exponential distribution with that rate

items.name: NormalPair
items.signature: pub func NormalPair<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, first: *var float64, second: *var float64)

doc.summary: A pair of independent standard normal values.
doc.markdown:
A pair of independent standard normal values.
The Box-Muller transform, which produces two at a time from two uniform draws — so this returns both rather
than throwing one away. The radial draw is taken on `1 - u` for the same reason as the exponential: the
logarithm of an exact zero is an infinity, and the generator will produce an exact zero eventually.
The polar form of the transform avoids the trigonometric functions at the cost of rejecting about a fifth of
its draws; this uses the direct form, which consumes a fixed two words and is therefore reproducible in a way
a rejection loop is not.

params.name: first
params.markdown: receives the first of the two draws

params.name: second
params.markdown: receives the second of the two draws

items.name: Normal
items.signature: pub func Normal<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> float64

doc.summary: A single standard normal value: mean zero, standard deviation one.
doc.markdown:
A single standard normal value: mean zero, standard deviation one.
Discards the second value of the pair. A caller drawing many should use `NormalPair` and keep both, which
halves the work.
doc.returns: a draw from the standard normal distribution

items.name: NormalWith
items.signature: pub func NormalWith<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, mean: float64, deviation: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A normal value with the given mean and standard deviation.
doc.markdown:
A normal value with the given mean and standard deviation.
A negative standard deviation is reflected rather than refused, since the distribution it describes is the
same one; a zero gives the mean exactly.
doc.returns: a draw from the normal distribution with that mean and deviation

items.name: FillBytes
items.signature: pub func FillBytes<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, into: var char8[..])

doc.summary: Fills `into` with random bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills `into` with random bytes.
The words are consumed least significant byte first, and a partial final word contributes its low bytes and
discards the rest — so the same `into.length` always consumes the same number of words, and two runs that
fill buffers of the same size stay in step.

items.name: NextUint32
items.signature: pub func NextUint32<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> uint32

doc.summary: The next 32-bit word: the low half of a 64-bit one.
doc.markdown:
The next 32-bit word: the low half of a 64-bit one.
A whole word is consumed and half of it discarded, which costs nothing and keeps the word stream aligned --
a generator that handed out the halves in turn would produce different sequences depending on how many
narrow draws happened to precede a wide one.
doc.returns: the next 32 bits

items.name: NextUint16
items.signature: pub func NextUint16<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> uint16

doc.summary: The next 16-bit word.
doc.markdown: The next 16-bit word.
doc.returns: the next 16 bits

items.name: NextUint8
items.signature: pub func NextUint8<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> uint8

doc.summary: The next 8-bit word.
doc.markdown: The next 8-bit word.
doc.returns: the next 8 bits

items.name: NextUint128
items.signature: pub func NextUint128<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> uint128

doc.summary: The next 128-bit word, high half drawn first.
doc.markdown: The next 128-bit word, high half drawn first.
doc.returns: the next 128 bits

items.name: NextFloat64
items.signature: pub func NextFloat64<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> float64

doc.summary: A `float64` uniformly distributed in `[0, 1)`.
doc.markdown:
A `float64` uniformly distributed in `[0, 1)`.
Built from the top 53 bits of a word, which is exactly the number a `float64` can hold without rounding: every
value produced is a multiple of 2^-53, each equally likely, and none is ever exactly one. Dividing a whole
word by 2^64 instead would round — and rounding upward at the top would produce exactly one, which callers
scaling into an array index do not expect.
doc.returns: a value in `[0, 1)`, with 53 bits of significance

items.name: NextFloat32
items.signature: pub func NextFloat32<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G) -> float32

doc.summary: A `float32` uniformly distributed in `[0, 1)`, from the top 24 bits.
doc.markdown: A `float32` uniformly distributed in `[0, 1)`, from the top 24 bits.
doc.returns: a value in `[0, 1)`, with 24 bits of significance

items.name: DirectMethodLimit
items.signature: pub const DirectMethodLimit: float64

doc.summary: Below this the direct methods are cheaper than the reductions, and above it they stop being practical.
doc.markdown: Below this the direct methods are cheaper than the reductions, and above it they stop being practical.

items.name: Gamma
items.signature: pub func Gamma<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, shape: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A value from the gamma distribution with the given shape and unit scale.
doc.markdown:
A value from the gamma distribution with the given shape and unit scale.
Marsaglia and Tsang's method: a normal draw squeezed through a cube, which accepts on the first attempt more
than ninety-five percent of the time for any shape at or above one. A shape below one is generated from a
shape one larger and scaled down, since the density is unbounded at zero there and the squeeze does not hold.
A shape at or below zero has no distribution and gives zero.
doc.returns: a draw from the gamma distribution with that shape and scale one

items.name: GammaWithScale
items.signature: pub func GammaWithScale<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, shape: float64, scale: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A value from the gamma distribution with the given shape and scale.
doc.markdown: A value from the gamma distribution with the given shape and scale.
doc.returns: a draw from the gamma distribution with that shape and scale

items.name: Beta
items.signature: pub func Beta<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, first: float64, second: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A value from the beta distribution with the two given shapes, in `[0, 1]`.
doc.markdown:
A value from the beta distribution with the two given shapes, in `[0, 1]`.
Built from two gamma draws, which is the definition rather than an approximation of it. Two shapes that are
both zero leave nothing to divide and give a half.
doc.returns: a draw from the beta distribution with those two shape parameters

items.name: RandomGenerator
items.signature: pub interface RandomGenerator

doc.summary: A source of uniformly distributed 64-bit words.
doc.markdown:
A source of uniformly distributed 64-bit words.
The single operation every generator supplies. Implementations must advance their own state, so the receiver
is a mutable reference. Borrowed interface views and generic bounds both keep it the caller's state that
advances.

doc.summary: The next 64-bit word, and the state advanced past it.
doc.markdown: The next 64-bit word, and the state advanced past it.
doc.returns: the next 64 bits

items.name: SplitMix64
items.signature: pub struct SplitMix64

doc.summary: The seeding generator: a fast mixer with a 64-bit state, used to spread one seed over a larger one.
doc.markdown:
The seeding generator: a fast mixer with a 64-bit state, used to spread one seed over a larger one.
Not for general use — its period is only 2^64 and it fails statistical tests a real generator passes. Its
job is the one thing it is very good at: turning a seed a human chose, which is very likely to be zero or
one or a timestamp, into a full-entropy state for a generator that deserves better input than that. Seeding
a 256-bit generator by copying a small integer into one word and leaving the rest zero is a classic way to
get correlated streams out of an excellent algorithm.

doc.summary: A mixer starting from `seed`.
doc.markdown: A mixer starting from `seed`. Every seed is acceptable, including zero.

params.name: seed
params.markdown: the value the generator starts from

doc.returns: a generator seeded with that value

doc.summary: The next word: the state advanced by an odd constant, then avalanched.
doc.markdown:
The next word: the state advanced by an odd constant, then avalanched.
The additive step guarantees the full period of 2^64 whatever the seed, and the mixing afterwards is
what turns a counter into something that looks random. Both constants are Steele, Lea and Flood's.
doc.returns: the next 64 bits

items.name: PcgMultiplier
items.signature: pub const PcgMultiplier: uint64

doc.summary: The multiplier used by both the state step and the output function.
doc.markdown:
The multiplier used by both the state step and the output function.
PCG's "cheap" 64-bit multiplier, which the DXSM variant uses in the 128-bit step as well.

items.name: Pcg64Dxsm
items.signature: pub struct Pcg64Dxsm

doc.summary: A PCG64-DXSM generator.
doc.markdown: A PCG64-DXSM generator.

doc.summary: A generator seeded by spreading `seed` through `SplitMix64`, on the default stream.
doc.markdown: A generator seeded by spreading `seed` through `SplitMix64`, on the default stream.

params.name: seed
params.markdown: the value the generator starts from

doc.returns: a generator seeded with that value, on the default stream

members.name: WithStream
members.signature: pub func WithStream(seed: uint64, stream: uint64) -> Pcg64Dxsm

doc.summary: A generator on the stream `stream` selects.
doc.markdown:
A generator on the stream `stream` selects.
Two generators with the same seed and different streams produce unrelated sequences of the same period,
which is how independent parallel streams are made without the workers having to agree on anything but
their own index.

params.name: seed
params.markdown: the value the generator starts from

params.name: stream
params.markdown: which of the generator's independent sequences to draw from

doc.returns: a generator seeded with that value, on the given stream

doc.summary: The next word.
doc.markdown:
The next word.
The output is computed from the state before it advances. The high half is folded twice and then
multiplied by the low half forced odd — an odd multiplier is invertible, so that last step permutes the
value rather than collapsing any of it.
doc.returns: the next 64 bits

items.name: Reservoir
items.signature: pub struct Reservoir<T>

doc.summary: A reservoir sample being built.
doc.markdown:
A reservoir sample being built.
Offer every item of the stream in turn and the reservoir ends holding a uniformly chosen subset of whatever
arrived, each subset of that size equally likely. The caller owns the storage, and its length is the sample
size.

fields.name: room
fields.doc: Where the sample is kept; its length is the sample size.

fields.name: seen
fields.doc: How many items have been offered so far.

members.name: Reservoir
members.signature: pub func Reservoir(room: var T[..]) -> Reservoir<T>

doc.summary: A reservoir that will fill `room`.
doc.markdown: A reservoir that will fill `room`.

params.name: room
params.markdown: how many items the reservoir keeps

doc.returns: an empty reservoir that will keep `room` items

doc.summary:
How many items the reservoir currently holds, which is the smaller of the sample size and the number
offered.
doc.markdown:
How many items the reservoir currently holds, which is the smaller of the sample size and the number
offered.
doc.returns: how many items it currently holds

doc.summary: How many items have been offered.
doc.markdown: How many items have been offered.
doc.returns: how many items have been offered to it in total

items.name: Offer
items.signature: pub func Offer<G: RandomGenerator, T>(generator: &var G, reservoir: &var Reservoir<T>, item: T)

doc.summary: Offers `item` to `reservoir`.
doc.markdown:
Offers `item` to `reservoir`.
Algorithm R: while the reservoir has room the item is kept outright, and afterwards the item replaces a
uniformly chosen existing entry with probability equal to the sample size over the number seen. That is what
keeps every subset equally likely at every moment, not merely at the end — so a stream can be cut short and
the sample is still uniform over what arrived.

params.name: reservoir
params.markdown: the reservoir to offer the item to

items.name: Shuffle
items.signature: pub func Shuffle<G: RandomGenerator, T>(generator: &var G, items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Shuffles `items` into a uniformly random order.
doc.markdown:
Shuffles `items` into a uniformly random order.
Fisher and Yates' method, walking from the end and swapping each position with one at or below it. The bound
is what makes it uniform: swapping with a position anywhere in the collection is the version that is subtly
biased, and it is the version almost everyone writes first.
Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.

params.name: items
params.markdown: the sequence to shuffle in place

items.name: ChooseIndex
items.signature: pub func ChooseIndex<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, count: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: A uniformly chosen index below `count`, or `count` itself when there is nothing to choose from.
doc.markdown:
A uniformly chosen index below `count`, or `count` itself when there is nothing to choose from.
Returning the count for an empty collection gives the caller a value that cannot be mistaken for a valid
index, which a zero would be.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many there are to choose among

doc.returns: an index in `[0, count)`, each equally likely

items.name: WeightedIndex
items.signature: pub func WeightedIndex<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, weights: float64[..]) -> uint

doc.summary: An index chosen in proportion to `weights`.
doc.markdown:
An index chosen in proportion to `weights`.
A weight of zero is never chosen; negative weights are treated as zero rather than subtracting from the
total, since a negative probability has no meaning and silently reversing a comparison is worse than
ignoring the entry. Weights that are all zero, or an empty slice, give the length — the same
out-of-range answer `ChooseIndex` gives for an empty collection.
Runs in time proportional to the length, reading the weights twice: once to total them and once to select.

params.name: weights
params.markdown: the relative weight of each index; they need not sum to one

doc.returns: an index chosen in proportion to its weight

items.name: XoshiroFromEntropy
items.signature: pub func XoshiroFromEntropy() -> Xoshiro256 ! EntropyError

doc.summary: A `Xoshiro256` seeded from the operating system's entropy.
doc.markdown:
A `Xoshiro256` seeded from the operating system's entropy.
Fails with why the entropy could not be obtained. A caller that is content with a predictable generator when
the system has no entropy recovers explicitly, as in `XoshiroFromEntropy() catch { else => Xoshiro256(0u64) }`.
doc.returns: a generator seeded from the system, or why it could not be seeded

items.name: PcgFromEntropy
items.signature: pub func PcgFromEntropy() -> Pcg64Dxsm ! EntropyError

doc.summary: A `Pcg64Dxsm` seeded from the operating system's entropy, on the default stream.
doc.markdown:
A `Pcg64Dxsm` seeded from the operating system's entropy, on the default stream.
Fails and recovers exactly as `XoshiroFromEntropy` does.
doc.returns: a generator seeded from the system, or why it could not be seeded

items.name: PcgFromEntropyWithStream
items.signature: pub func PcgFromEntropyWithStream(stream: uint64) -> Pcg64Dxsm ! EntropyError

doc.summary: A `Pcg64Dxsm` seeded from entropy on the stream `stream` selects.
doc.markdown:
A `Pcg64Dxsm` seeded from entropy on the stream `stream` selects.
The intended shape for parallel work: every worker calls this with its own index, so the streams are
independent by construction and the whole run is reproducible from the one seed if it is recorded.

params.name: stream
params.markdown: which of the generator's independent sequences to draw from

doc.returns: a generator on that stream seeded from the system, or why it could not be seeded

items.name: UniformBelow
items.signature: pub func UniformBelow<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, bound: uint64) -> uint64

doc.summary: A uniform value in `[0, bound)`.
doc.markdown:
A uniform value in `[0, bound)`.
A bound of zero has no values to choose from and gives zero, which is the only answer that is not a lie.
Runs in constant expected time; the loop below runs more than once with probability under `bound / 2^64`.
doc.returns: a value in `[0, bound)`, each equally likely and with no modulo bias

items.name: UniformInRange
items.signature: pub func UniformInRange<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, low: uint64, high: uint64) -> uint64

doc.summary: A uniform value in `[low, high]`, both ends included.
doc.markdown:
A uniform value in `[low, high]`, both ends included.
Inclusive because that is what a caller asking for a die roll or a random index into a known last element
means. `low` above `high` is an empty range and gives `low`. The full range of the type is representable:
a span of every value is a bound of 2^64, which does not fit in a `uint64`, and is handled as its own case
rather than by an arithmetic accident.
doc.returns: a value in `[low, high)`, each equally likely

items.name: UniformInSignedRange
items.signature: pub func UniformInSignedRange<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, low: int64, high: int64) -> int64

doc.summary: A uniform signed value in `[low, high]`, both ends included.
doc.markdown:
A uniform signed value in `[low, high]`, both ends included.
The span is computed in unsigned arithmetic, so a range crossing zero — or spanning the whole width, where
the difference of the ends overflows a signed type — is ordinary rather than a special case.
doc.returns: a value in `[low, high)`, each equally likely

items.name: UniformFloatInRange
items.signature: pub func UniformFloatInRange<G: RandomGenerator>(generator: &var G, low: float64, high: float64) -> float64

doc.summary: A uniform `float64` in `[low, high)`.
doc.markdown:
A uniform `float64` in `[low, high)`.
The interval is half-open at the top, matching `NextFloat64`. A reversed pair gives `low`, and an interval so
wide that its span overflows to an infinity gives values across the whole of it rather than a NaN.
doc.returns: a value in `[low, high)`

items.name: Xoshiro256
items.signature: pub struct Xoshiro256

doc.summary: A Xoshiro256** generator.
doc.markdown: A Xoshiro256** generator.

doc.summary: A generator seeded by spreading `seed` through `SplitMix64`.
doc.markdown:
A generator seeded by spreading `seed` through `SplitMix64`.
Every seed is acceptable, zero included: the mixer's output is what fills the state, and it cannot
produce four zero words from any seed. Seeding by copying the seed into one word and leaving the rest
zero — which is what a caller does by hand — gives a state so close to the fixed point that the first
several outputs are visibly poor, which is the whole reason this goes through the mixer.

params.name: seed
params.markdown: the value the generator starts from

doc.returns: a generator seeded with that value

doc.summary: A generator from four words of state given directly, for reproducing a stream recorded elsewhere.
doc.markdown:
A generator from four words of state given directly, for reproducing a stream recorded elsewhere.
An all-zero state is the one state with no future, so it is replaced by the mixer's output for a zero
seed rather than accepted into a generator that would return zero forever.

params.name: words
params.markdown: the generator's state words, taken as they are

doc.returns: a generator with exactly those state words

doc.summary: The next word.
doc.markdown:
The next word.
The result is computed from the state *before* it advances, which is the published order and the reason
two implementations agree on the first word rather than being one step apart forever.
doc.returns: the next 64 bits
